{{Short description|Equation used in general relativity}}
{{Distinguish|Nernst equation}}

In [[general relativity]], the '''Ernst equation'''<ref>[https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ErnstEquation.html Weisstein, Eric W, ''Ernst equation,'' MathWorld--A Wolfram Web.]</ref> is an [[Integrable system|integrable]] [[non-linear partial differential equation]], named after the American [[physicist]] {{ill|Frederick J. Ernst|sl|Frederick Joseph Ernst}} who published it in 1968.<ref>Ernst, F. J. (1968). New formulation of the axially symmetric gravitational field problem. Physical Review, 167(5), 1175.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://mypages.iit.edu/~segre/iit_physics_bios/ernst_f.html |title=Biography of Frederick J. Ernst |access-date=2017-05-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180104233406/http://mypages.iit.edu/~segre/iit_physics_bios/ernst_f.html |archive-date=2018-01-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Description==

The Ernst's equation governing the complex scalar function <math>Z</math> is given by<ref>Chandrasekhar, S. (1998). The mathematical theory of black holes (Vol. 69). Oxford university press.</ref>

:<math>\Re(Z)\nabla^2 Z = \nabla Z \cdot \nabla Z</math>

where <math>\nabla</math> is the two-dimensional gradient operator with axisymmetry; for instance, if <math>Z=Z(\rho,z)</math>, then

<math display="block"> \Re(Z)\left[\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial }{\partial\rho}\left(\rho\frac{\partial Z}{\partial\rho}\right)+ \frac{\partial^2 Z}{\partial^2 z}\right] = \left(\frac{\partial Z}{\partial \rho}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial Z}{\partial z}\right)^2.</math>

and  if <math>Z=Z(t,\rho)</math> (with <math>c=1</math>), then<ref>Chandrasekhar, S. (1986). Cylindrical waves in general relativity. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences, 408(1835), 209-232.</ref>

<math display="block"> \Re(Z)\left[ \frac{\partial^2 Z}{\partial^2 t}-\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial }{\partial\rho}\left(\rho\frac{\partial Z}{\partial\rho}\right)\right] = \left(\frac{\partial Z}{\partial t}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial Z}{\partial \rho}\right)^2.</math>

where <math display="inline"> \Re(Z)</math> is the real part of <math display="inline">Z</math>. If <math>Z</math> is a solution of the Ernst's equation, then <math>Z/(1+icZ)</math> (so is <math>Z^{-1}</math>) is also a solution where <math>c</math> is an arbitrary real constant. The transformation <math>Z\to Z/(1+icZ)</math> belongs to the so-called '''Ehlers transformation'''.

Often, one introduces

:<math>Z = -\frac{1+E}{1-E}</math>

so that we have

:<math>(1-|E|^2) \nabla^2 E = - 2 E^* \nabla E\cdot \nabla E.</math>

The Ernst equation is derivable from the Lagrangian density

:<math>\mathcal{L}=\frac{\nabla Z\cdot \nabla Z}{\Re(Z)^2}=\frac{\nabla E\cdot \nabla E^*}{(1-|E|)^2}.</math>

For its [[Lax pair]] and other features see e.g.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Harrison | first=B. Kent | title=Bäcklund Transformation for the Ernst Equation of General Relativity | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=41 | issue=18 | date=30 October 1978 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.41.1197 | pages=1197–1200| bibcode=1978PhRvL..41.1197H }}</ref><ref>{{cite conference|last=Marvan |first=M. |year=2004 |title=Recursion operators for vacuum Einstein equations with symmetries |conference=Proceedings of the Conference on Symmetry in nonlinear mathematical physics| location=Kyiv, Ukraine|arxiv=nlin/0401014|journal=Proceedings of the Institute of Mathematics of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine|volume=50|pages=179–183}}</ref> and references therein.

== Usage ==
The ''Ernst equation'' is employed in order to produce exact solutions of the [[Einstein's equations]] in the [[general theory of relativity]].
